messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Malia was fifty-three when her husband Kimo died—not from illness or age, but from a drunk driver who ran a red light three blocks from their home. She had been closing her small gift shop that evening, the one she and Kimo had opened together fifteen years earlier, when the police called. She never made it to the hospital in time. For weeks afterward, the shock dulled everything, but then the details began to surface in fragments she could not control: the phone ringing, the drive, the way the chaplain’s voice sounded hollow. Even now, more than a year later, she cannot tell the story from beginning to end without gaps—the memory forces its way into her mind like a film that plays over and over, but the scenes are out of order, the middle missing, the end always the same. After the memory had surfaced, even the most ordinary things — a kettle whistling, a door slamming — felt like warnings she couldn't afford to ignore.

The smell of alcohol is the worst. A customer walking in with beer on his breath, or a bottle of whiskey being shelved near the counter, and suddenly Malia is back at the intersection, the paramedics, the stretcher. Her heart pounds, her hands shake, and she feels as if she is in danger right there in her own shop, even though nothing is actually wrong. She has come to believe that she cannot relax anywhere, not even at home with the door locked, because the danger could come from anywhere at any time—a thought that feels utterly rational when the flashback hits. Already running on that sense of threat, she found that almost anything could tip into a warning — a van parked at an odd angle, a light left on that shouldn't have been. When someone mentions losing a loved one, even in passing, the same thing happens: her chest tightens, and the film starts rolling again. She has stopped attending funerals and avoids the cemetery altogether, because those places do not just remind her of Kimo; they convince her that her life has been destroyed and that there is no future left.

Malia’s negative appraisals have become a self-fulfilling trap. She feels she does not know herself anymore—the woman who once laughed easily, who ran the shop with pride, who believed in hard work and tomorrows. Now she sees herself as someone whose story ended the night Kimo died. That hopelessness makes her hypervigilant; she scans every customer’s face, every car pulling into the lot, for signs of threat. It also colours her memory: when the intrusive images come, they are not just painful—they confirm that she has nothing ahead, that the past is all there is. And because she expects to be triggered, she finds triggers everywhere. A casual remark about a friend’s recent loss, a glimpse of a funeral notice in the newspaper, and she is pulled back into the loop, her negative appraisals deepening each time.

The shop itself has become a minefield. The alcohol section is at the back, and Malia now keeps that aisle dimly lit, stocking it only when she knows no one else is around. She has snapped at customers who commented on her husband’s death after seeing a photo on the counter, and she dreads the annual grief-awareness display the local hospital puts up in the window. She avoids answering the phone if she does not recognise the number, afraid it will be news of another death. The false alarms come daily: a car backfiring, a sudden shout, even the smell of flowers from the arrangement a regular brought in last week—each one sends her heart racing and convinces her that something terrible is about to happen again.

What finally brought Malia to seek help was a moment last month when she realised she had stopped ordering new inventory. She had let the shop run on fumes, barely opening some days, because the thought of facing another customer, another possible trigger, felt impossible. She sat in the back room, looking at a box of Kimo’s old shirts she still could not donate, and she thought, *I have no future*. That recognition frightened her more than any flashback. She made an appointment with a therapist because she is afraid of what she will become if she does not—but she is also afraid that nothing can change, that the film will keep playing, and that the woman she used to be is gone for good.
